projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Denny Frangos was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Denny Frangos. Mr. Frangos served in the U.S. Navy Seabees with the 77th Construction Battalion. He served in the Pacific Theater and his highest rank was construction mate 3rd class. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Frangos' home in Willoughby Hills, Ohio on March 15, 2005. Denny was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Good morning.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: 3588 East 116 Street, Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: At that time I was--

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (female)
sp.p: Eighteen.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Nineteen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nineteen?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were you out of school in--

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: --in '41? Were you working?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: I was working at the National Acme Company as a welder.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh. Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, I went out in the backyard. I had a 1937 Ford and I was changing the oil on it. And I got a little porch on the second floor and my father stuck his head out and he, he said, the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor. And I didn't know what he was talking about, I never heard of Pearl Harbor and that was it. And then he said, you don't understand, son. He says, the United States is gonna go to war, and he was right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what did you think when that sank in and you realized we were in the war?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: I didn't think too much because the department I was working at, at National Acme, they were--that department was making armor purser bullets on the automatic screw machines and I didn't think much about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So would that give you--that would give you an exemption from the draft then?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: I had an exemption but my, my, friend who went to high school with me and worked with me over there--he said, "let's enlist," and I said "okay." He said, "I want to enlist in the Marines," I said "well, I want to enlist in the Navy." So we went down and they says, why don't you join the Seabees, that's a combination, Seabees, I mean, Navy and Marines. So I said, "What is the Seabees." (Laughing)--so we enlisted in the Seabees and we--they sent us home because the camp wasn't built yet. So about a month and a half later I got a call to go to Camp Perry in Virginia, on the Chesapeake Bay. And Jim and I went, and the second day there we were marching from our barracks to the chow hall. I was the last guy in line and a truck--one of the Navy trucks came behind us--no brakes and they hit me in the elbow and broke my elbow. So I ended up in sick bay and that's when my friend and I got separated. And while I was in sick bay it was quarantined with the flu, so I got the flu. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: In--my papers say December 9, but I actually enlisted November 22nd or something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh. So you actually went in and--

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: But they called me January 9th or something like that--'43 to go to Virginia. Or to go downtown and grab a train.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: --huh-huh, so what else can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The training phase?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: We had rifle range training. We had obstacle course training. We had forest marches carrying heavy packs, going through slush and mud and setting up camps and hand-to-hand combat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was most of that done at that Camp Perry there?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, under the Marines. We were--we were sent to another section of the camp which was the Marine camp, and they were the ones that were training us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've heard that there were a lot of older guys that were in the Seabees?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yep. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, did they have a tough time with that training?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah they had, (Laughing)--yeah, they had a pretty tough time. In fact, one of the guys from Cleveland, Tony Ferandi(ph), he was 36. He could hardly, he could hardly carry the pack, let alone walk. So we all helped--everybody helped everybody. It was really nice. Except the rifle range, some of the older guys weren't that good. And I was, I was pretty good with the Thompson Submachine Gun, so that's what they gave me. I could take a drum of 50 bullets and throw out a five gallon can and hold it sideways without aiming and hit it 50 out of 50. He didn't believe me, but I showed him. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you were actually out there in the field, you weren't necessarily armed were you--when you were doing your work?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: You mean overseas?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Well, for the first few weeks, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Cause, when we usually went to a place, we usually went in right after the invasions.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Maybe a couple of days later on one of them and a couple of weeks later, but I mean--the front lines were always moving back-and-forth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think I'm getting ahead of myself, my fault. Umm, is there anything else you want to talk about your training before you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Well we went--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other instance you remember?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --yeah, we went from Virginia--we went up to Endicott Rhode Island, Quonset Point, and they didn't have any facilities at all. So we built a bus, or yeah, a bus station so people could go into town or go home or whatever. And they didn't have steel so we made it out of logs, wood, timber, heavy stuff. I understand it's still there. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Then from there we went to Port Whyneeme.(ph) Spelled H-u-e-n-e-m-e. Hueneme.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: We went to Port Hueneme, and on a troop train we passed right through Cleveland. And we stopped at 105th and Dupont--a bus or railroad stop there, and they were giving us sandwiches for lunch. I opened up the window so I can talk to some people, you know, tell them, phone my parents and tell them I'm coming through. And when I did that a .45 (Laughing)--poked me right in the nose and told me to get back in. They didn't want anybody to know we were going through. And we went from there cross-country, and we stopped at Texas. And it was--we were right in the middle of a desert somewhere and they made no arrangements for food and we were starving. So they stopped at this small town outside of Amarillo and somebody went into town and got a hamburger joint there to make a thousand hamburgers for us. They brought em back. And then from there we went to Port Hueneme. And from there we left and we went overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So about when did you head overseas?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Must have been about July 1943 or June.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: But when we left Port Hueneme, we left on a single ship. No convoys or anything. We were all alone and we zigzagged all over the Pacific for about two weeks. And one day--one early morning, the captain--and the ship was the MS Weldervraden,(ph) Motor Ship Weldervraden.(ph) It was a Dutch banana boat with a Dutch captain and a Dutch crew, but a U.S. Navy gun crew. And he saw a wake of a torpedo coming at us. He put one screw in reverse and the other in forward and swung that ship around 90 degrees. Everybody fell down and he went in the opposite direction. No zigzag, straight as fast as that ship could go. And that ship was a very fast ship, because it was used to deliver bananas from the Caribbean to, to Holland. So it had to do it in a day and a half or two days so--and then the return trip was nice and slow. It had a diesel engine. That thing was fast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And it had--probably had to be fast so the bananas wouldn't rot?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, that's why it was fast. So it happened to be stuck over in Borneo someplace--the Dutch East Indies. When the Japanese went there--so the Navy took it over. They leased it I guess, and they used it for us and I guess he took us about a week out of our position. So it took us four weeks to get to New Caledonia and then, then from there we picked up supplies and we went to Guadalcanal, and we got there early morning and had--and it was a full moon that week. And if you were on a ship in the harbor at night with a full moon, you knew you were gonna get bombed because we didn't have--we had Henderson Field where we had very few planes and they had Rabaul, Kavieng and their airfields on Bougainville. They were sending planes down all the time, by the fifties and hundreds. And when we got there at Guadalcanal we started to unload and it was getting dusk and that captain said, "that's it, everybody off." He turned around and left with a lot of our food and so forth. He wasn't gonna to hang around for nighttime. And that night, like he--he was worried, we got bombed and in the morning we had more casualties going to sick bay; cuts and bruises and broken bones. Because we pitched up our tents and between each tent was supposed to be a slit, trench, for you to jump into during an air raid, but if there were any roots or stones or coral or something, they put it on the other side and they pitched the tents a little bit closer together so that the guidelines came crisscross. Well, you didn't know that if you just happened to be standing around when an air raid started. So you took a dive to go in-between and you ended up splitting your fingers on those tent stakes (Laughing)--and guys were throwing broken bottles out there so you ended up on that. Nobody got hurt by the air raid but a lot of people got hurt the other way--the more stitches and more broken bones. And, and later on when we went to Vella LaVella I was on a, I was on a LST, LST-167. It was a Coast Guard operated landing ship and as we were approaching Vella LaVella two Japanese came--planes--and they dropped a 500 pound bomb right through the flying bridge and it went right down inside cruise quarters and blew up. Killed about 40, 45. Most of it was crew members. A lot of it were--some were our guys, some were the Marines, cause we had 150 of our guys on there with our equipment, our food. Most of it was food and water. And there was 150 Marines and us. And behind us, out in the bay were what they call APD's. These were the old World War I, four-stack destroyers. They just used it to carry passengers, and they had 250 Marines on each one. Well, we had two P-38's as escort. And when the two Japanese planes came over they headed out toward the APD's and these two P-38's went after the--around and came back and started strafing at us. We were, I would say maybe 600 feet from the shore when the bombs hit. Luckily, we had the doors open this way, but the ramp didn't come down yet. There was a crew member, I could see him through the flames. He was cranking it, hand operating the crank to let the ramp down so we can jump off, and the water was like as high as this ceiling, eight feet or so. I jumped off into the, into the water that was burning--had fuel on top burning. I went right to the bottom and I walked, and every once in a while when I couldn't hold my breath any for, any more, I came up and broke the surface. Came up this way, took a deep breath, went back down--and I wouldn't let go of my Thompson cuz that's--might have been a little heavy, but that was my protection and in fact, right here you can see my ear got burned. See that little lump right here?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Right on the tip, right here, my ear got burned. What your supposed to do is when you come up you go like this, and open it up so the burning gasoline would, would open up. And when you come up, you come up this way--go back down and the second or the third time I came up I was--I wasn't making much progress. Some guy was swimming by (Laughing)--and we were in the clear water now. Boomer, one of our guys, I said, "hey Boomer," I said "I can't swim." He said, "jump on." So I did, like a horse (Laughing)--I jumped right on him and he took me in. Well, when I got waist deep I got off. I went in--my clothes were burned and there was a young Marine, he looked like he was about 17 years old, a little blond haired kid--dead, on the beach. But he was my size--I opened up his pack and I took a shirt and pants because mine were burned. The tips of my fingers were burned from coming up like this and this ear. So then I was--I was the personal bodyguard for an Australian who had lived on that island as a plantation supervisor for coconut trees.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Name was Mr. Gill, G-i-l-l, Gill. He was a great big six-foot-four guy, but he wouldn't take a gun for self-preservation. But he insisted on going because he knew that island and we had no aerial maps except tree tops, and that didn't tell you what was underneath. So we knew nothing about the topal of the island. So, he sat in on the plans and he knew what was going on and nobody else did. And they were afraid if the Japanese captured him, they'd learn about our going up further and the dates. So they had me and another guy as his bodyguard, and if it looks like he's gonna get captured, shoot him. He was a real nice guy, I wouldn't do that. But he knew of a nice cave in the coral. About, about six--five or six foot high and about eight foot deep. Real nice dry cave. So we headed for that, because at nighttime with that burning LST beached, that was a good landmark for the next wave of bombers to come over, which they did. They bombed all our equipment and everything that we happened to land. The only thing we saved as far as food goes were these five gallon tins of fruit cocktail (Coughing)--that's what we had to eat for a week. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What island was this again?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Vella LaVella.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Ok, was that near New Caledonia or--

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, no. No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: --pretty far away. I'll check my map.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: See here, here's New Caledonia, and here's Guadalcanal and there's Vella LaVella.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay, so this is northeast of Australia. Well, actually almost due east.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: It was north of New Caledonia.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And then we went from there we went to Bougainville and we built a bomber field.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Well--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh you know, before we get into that, how did you eventually get rescued from Vella LaVella?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --well we, we got off of that, or we--later on about a week later, more LST's with the rest of--cause we were the, the forward echelon, so they came up later with all the equipment and the food, cooks and everything else, and they--see when we went there that was originally--that was the Japanese radio station. They'd radio Rabaul--let 'em know if we were sending planes over or ships to bomb them so that they can prepare and bomb us and--the thing is they had the ships and the planes and we didn't. And there was a 60 man radio crew--they, they figured, was a 600 man crew on the island. So they sent over 400 Marines, 150 with us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And prior to us--about three or four days they sent over 600 New Zealanders and the New Zealanders spent most of their time setting up their camp, not scouting the island. So they wanted us to do that. And then we found out that the New Zealanders had the Mores, the natives. They were like the Hawaiian's.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Big husky guys, real nice guys. In the daytime strongest guys you ever saw. In the nighttime especially with the full moon they were afraid of their own shadow. You couldn't get 'em out of their tents. They were so scared. It was just the way they were brought up, superstitious. Real nice guys. Daytime they would go out and shoot anybody that they could find, cut off their heads and bring it back (Laughing)--they'd hang it up over their tents.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And--but at night they were scared. And then from there-- after we built an airfield and a hospital. That's the first thing we'd do when we went somewhere. We'd build a hospital and a chow hall--a place to eat and a place for injured and sick. Cause there was a lot of sickness from malaria and dysentery. In fact, I had pleurisy from sleeping on the ground. You're supposed to sleep high and dry, but if you didn't get the chance you had to sleep on the ground.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Jungle rot?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yes, jungle rot and we got to Bougainville and we went way in the back of Empress Agusta Bay up against the foothills of the mountains. The Japanese had the, the hill, we didn't. And we built a bomber field there, Peeva(ph) P-i-v-a. These were for big airplanes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: There was a small airfield up at the beach Torokina. That was for the fighter planes. And while we were working on there a TBF which is a torpedo fighter bomber--a biggest single engine plane in the Navy came in to land--and there was a volcanic ash. The whole basin was a volcanic ash; powder--black powder. Got stuck in his brakes and one wheel locked and the other didn't. He made an abrupt turn and I was on, on a back end of a bulldozer, shooting up at the mountain. Every time we reached a certain point, they were taking potshots at the driver. So, to keep them down--when we got to that point, I had a plate up here and a B-A-R and I just ta-ta-ta-ta, ta-ta-ta-ta, just anywhere on the hill.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Keep them down. So when we passed that point we were okay. And then, while I'm looking over here, I ain't looking back there and this plane came in. The hub of the propeller hit the driver right in the face. Broke his neck and the wing. Below the wing where the wheel wells were, hit me here and broke a couple of ribs. This is after I had pleurisy and with pleurisy they tape you up because you can't inhale deeply--and they took the tape off and I was healing real good. Wham. There goes a couple of ribs. (Laughing) So then they'd tape me up again. I couldn't stand up, I couldn't even go to chow. People were bringing the chow to me. And then--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the driver survive?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --did what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the driver of that bulldozer--did he survive?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, he--he just had a broken neck but they sent him to New Caledonia to a hospital and then--when a month or so later when he was okay they took the thing off--the brace off his neck. They sent him back to us instead of sending him home. (Laughing) And then Tom Florio(ph)--and then in April I guess it was--yeah, April. They got wind--somehow they found out that the Japanese were gonna, gonna assemble at the top of the hill and come charging down across the field, burn up all the airplanes and kill anybody they can across there. Way down over there was the 72nd Seabees and we're the 77th Seabees up at this end of the bomber field. And when they found out about this--the Marine, 3rd Marine Defense Battalion dug a big round hole over here and setup sandbags with the--a machine gun here and a machine gun there. Four places along the field on the field of 7,000 feet long because it was for, for a four-engine liberators. We had liberators there that would fly north to Truk which was the biggest Navy--Japanese Navy base in the area and you couldn't get near it because they'd sink you or shoot you down. This plane which, which had a very long range, it was a liberator with a single tail like a B-17 instead of a twin tail. And the Navy called it the Privateer, but it was a four-engine bomber converted to take photographs from high altitudes. So it would fly over there, circle around, take some pictures and fly back, which was further than a B-17 could go. And the Japanese wanted that airplane, so they sent 1,500 guys down yelling and screaming at everything. Well when we knew that what they were gonna do--we cleared during the night--we went out and cleared the jungle for about 300 feet, cleared all the--left the big trees and took all the little saplings out and the foliage and we put coiled barbed wire--and back about a hundred feet or little more--then we put X-shaped rods that we drove into the ground and we put tucked barbed wire on this side over there in the middle--and on the bottom--tight all the way across about three feet high and then another hundred and something feet back we just had a single wire on top and a single wire on the bottom which were about two feet apart, and we had our 600 volt generator hooked up to it. (Laughing)--And then over here we had like flare guns that would shoot star shells and stick it in the tree--it had--like a dart--would stick over here and it would burn and light up the whole area. So when they came down (shooting sound) all those star shells went up. They called us out to go on our side of the bomber field. We had trenches dug all the way across there and there we are, we're sitting there like this. They never got over to our side. We killed--all you heard were those machine guns going. And we could see at the other side--we could see people trying to climb over all that wire. You couldn't make out the features but you could see like, like, almost like a silhouette. And we had what they call a sound power unit. It wasn't hooked up to power but it was wired to the machine guns. And when you talked you generated power so that the other side would hear. They were sitting over there. Hey, over on the left side is a guy trying to climb over and then they would turn their gun around and shoot till they get 'em. You got 'em. (Laughing) In the morning when we got up we went out there. Over 1,500 were killed. And what we did--we dug a big trench, pushed them in, counted the legs, divided by two and covered it up. And then the next night the dummies tried the same thing. So the next night we got--we got 1,500 the first time and 400 the second night. Then they gave up and then what they did, they stayed on over the other side of the crest of the hill. Which is the, the--it was the foot of the mountain. In fact, over there was a volcano; Mt. Bagana, which gave us an earthquake (Laughing)--Christmas Eve. That was our Christmas present--was a big earthquake. And then--so instead of coming over the top of the hill to come down and burn up the airplanes, they just started--use trench mortars. They were mortaring us. They knew--they can tell. They--I guess they watched what--with glasses, binoculars, your chow hall. Your chow time is twelve to one so that's where all the guys are going to be in there eating, so we'll aim for the chow hall and if you don't hit the chow hall, aim for the trees, so a tree burst will send all the shrapnel down and sure enough that worked a couple of times. In fact, a good friend of mine got a big piece of shrapnel in his back and he was yelling how it hurt him and I saw his shirt was--a hole over here and I saw his skin. There was a hole over there--hardly no blood. A little puffed up, and I put my finger down it cause it was--smoke was coming out of it. I burned my finger, that thing was still in there, red hot. I told him to go to sick bay and get rid of it because it's still in there--piece of shrapnel. And then this liberator got hit by a mortar shell on the wing--well right next to the planes and their revetments we had these great big--oh bigger than a 55 gallon drum of CO2 on--like a carriage, great big wheels. So if anything happened, they'd wheel that out and shhh, shhh--put the fire out. Well, if we stole beer somewhere and you wanted to cool it, the best way to cool it is take a CO2 bottle and sprinkle it. So whenever we'd swipe some beer someplace we went over to the bomber field and squirted it until that big tank was empty. Well, they hit the wing, they'd go like this to put the fire out (Laughing)--there's no CO2, so they, they lost an airplane. And they lined us up along the airfield the next day, about noon, when it was real hot. The temperature out there and the humidity is way up there--but the temperature up in the 110, 120. We're out in the middle of the airfield with our sleeves rolled down standing at attention and an officer comes out and there's a canopy over his head and there's a fan, and he's nice and cool. And he's reading out of the articles of the government, governing of the Navy--the Blue Book about what could happen to you for doing what happened. Forty-five minutes we're standing at attention and listening to him; soaking wet. Guys are passing out cuz their--your legs get numb and everything. And if he passed out and fell over and you go to pick him up, he told you to stand at attention. At the very end, after about 45 minutes he says, now he says "I know why you did this, you wanted to cool off your beer." He says, "what's more important, a big airplane or a beer." Some idiot in the back yelled out "beer." We had another half hour of standing there. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that Halsey doing that speech?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it Admiral Halsey doing this speech?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I mean, that's so important. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: We were soaking wet but he wasn't--didn't have a drop of water on him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But Admiral Halsey happened to be there when that happened.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: He was angry. He didn't only line us up--he lined--there was us--there was the New Zealanders. There was the--part of the 37th Division, the 147th Infantry from Ohio. They were there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's a Four-Star Admiral, is my point.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: I forgot who else, but there must of been about 3,000 guys lined up. An idiot had to say beer. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) Halsey let 'em have it, huh?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah and when we were on Vella LaVella this piece of shrapnel over here--the plane was strafing us--this piece of shrapnel--or he hit something over there somewhere, or it could have been a Daisy Cutter Bomb. I don't know, but I--usually I'd--I only wore the plastic insert of the helmet. I didn't wear the steel because it was heavy and it was hot. I didn't need it and I usually hung that over here or left it in my tent because that's what you shaved in, washed your feet and everything. But I happened to have it here and I had no place else to carry other stuff, so--because I had another drum of 50 bullets. I hung that there and, took my helmet and I put it on because I had no place else to put it and I happen to look up and this thing is coming by, real slow. It looked like a butterfly and I was wondering--Wow. Bang. Hit the top of the helmet over here. Pushed it in--it cracked the liner and left a goose egg about that big, knocked me out. I felt like I got hit with a sledgehammer. And the helmet got dented up here and the plastic liner got busted. And I had like a baseball size lump over here. Well, I'm down and other guys tried to pull my helmet off. Whoa. Well they were trying to pull it off over that lump and it wasn't coming off too easy and the guys are screaming--you know, "any blood, any blood." "No, I don't see any blood." Well finally I, I woke up and I--"Hey don't pull--don't pull my helmet, that hurts" and I, I, I took it off this way--put my hand over here--Holy Mackeral--they looked--there were no breaks but boy there was a bump there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No purple heart, but I can't resist--

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: So this thing--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: --so this souvenir is a piece of shrapnel from that?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --yeah and that's the little piece. I wouldn't believe that this thing sounded or felt like a sledgehammer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Because it's light. Well he took it and he drilled a hole in it. He ground off the sharp edges but boy that was like a razor, all the way around it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: I picked it up and I--it was still hot. And, wow, I said what the hell could that be.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What a novelty, nobody will take it.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: "What could that be?" The guy said, "that came off your helmet." I said, "your kidding, this little thing made all that noise."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing)--What island?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: That was on Vella LaVella. That thing, I don't think it weighs two ounces.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What if a 30 caliber would have hit you in the head?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Well, while we were over there--no, we went to Emaru.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: Sniper.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, over on Bougainville a guy I went to high school with was with the 3rd Marine Defense Battalion down at the beach, and he used to come up to our chow hall. Their colonel was a guy that--his philosophy was, in order to be a good Marine you got to be a mean Marine. So I'm gonna give you only two meals, light meals a day and your gonna be hungry and your gonna be mean. That was his philosophy. So we--they were starving so we'd invite them--come over to our chow hall and eat. So after they were starting to shell us, in fact the first night--the first day they were shelling us he came with me to our chow hall and we were eating over at the far end--boom--blew right through the canvas roof--down in there. It exploded (Coughing)--hurt a couple of guys. Everybody took off and I said "Steve, where you going" I says, "Now's the time to eat, you got everything right here." He said "Oh no, I ain't hanging here," (Laughing)--he left. And then what we did then we changed our chow hall hours from eleven to twelve. At twelve o'clock, we hung up an empty oxygen tank and hit it with a hammer. When you heard that, ding-ding-ding--scram, leave the camp because their gonna bomb us. And, so then he'd come up at eleven o'clock he'd sit on the side of the road near our driveway until I came back and then--cuz, they couldn't go into our chow hall. They'd only come in with one of our members as a guest so--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's the name of the guy?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --Steve Banyes.(Ph)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And he was a Marine?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah. He was a Third Marine Defense Battalion. He went to high school with me. So then--oh, after about a week or so he would bring his friends from his tent. And a (Coughing)--one of them or two of them were sitting on the side--we had a--like a mound in front of our camp all the way around the road accept where the driveway was. And these guys would sit on that mound waiting for us to come in, to take 'em into our chow hall. But a couple of his buddies came--I'd already went into the chow hall with Steve and they were waiting to get picked up by somebody else. A mortar shell lands right there and kills two of them. Poor guys just wanted to get some food. And one of our guys over here in a tent--the shrapnel went all the way around--one spot over here like, like a semicircle was clean and clear--over there was peppered with holes. So everybody went in there and there's this guy on a cot unconscious. They figured he was hit and he was the chaplains assistant (Laughing)--on his, on his cot, he had a great big cross. Above that was full of holes and down here was where he was laying. Never got a scratch. Two guys got killed over here and a third guy was sitting on a Jeep hood. He got blown off to the other side of the road and that's--

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: Brian Keith.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --Brian Keith, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: My good 'ol buddy was telling me a little bit about him. Oh wow.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: He didn't--never got a scratch--he got blown off the Jeep--got scraped a little bit--never, never got hurt.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He used to always tell you how he was going to become a movie star and come visit, remember. Nobody would believe him.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And then, then we went to admiralties (ph)--no, no, we went to Emaru and we took--a mountain, all it was, was just a big semi-mountain sticking out of the ocean. So in order to make a fighter strip over there we had to cut the top of the mountain off. Put part of it here and part of it there. So that instead of being like this, we took this much off over to here, to over here and made it flat. And we built--we built a pretty good, nice fighter strip there. Over here is Rabaul. Right here and then up across the top is Kaveang. Rabaul was the big Navy base, big airbase. MR. SWOPE: (Continuing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: They had over 140,000 men and ships there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Right here. So what we were trying to do was encircle it and isolate it. Keep supplies from coming in, starving them. That was the whole reason for all of this. And the admiralties, I went with an advanced group as a welder because they were assembling--they were assembling a floating dry dock. Big enough to raise a battleship. It was a 10-section ABSD-2; Advanced Base Stationary Dry Dock number two. Ten sections long, about 900 feet long. The wing walls were 57 feet high from the deck. The deck was 15 feet above the water, so now your what, 72 feet--on top of that is a gantry crane with a 60 foot boom. Now your talking 130 feet up the air. This was big--made of barges all welded together. Each barge had a 10,000 horsepower pump at each end to bring in water, submerge-- they had divers put kill blocks under the ship and they tied the sides, dogged it down real good. Then the pumps would pump out the water, because the water would go all the way up into the wing wall. And the wing walls were 20 foot wide, 57 foot high, 80 feet this way. And so that's 20,000 horsepower pumps-- pumping out the water would raise the ship. (Coughing)--So I went to work on that, and one morning the idiot pilots from--I guess they were from Kaveang because that was the clearest, nearest Japanese air base--came over and they were gonna strafe and try to bomb and hurt whatever's over there. This is just after we put up--in fact I welded a 40-millimeter gun sponson so there were one, two, 40-millimeter guns and, one at each end of the wing wall and two, 20-millimeter on each side of the gun sponson so there was--each barge had four, 40-millimeter, eight, 20-millimeters times ten, so that's--on each side was 40, 20-millimeters and twenty, 40-millimeters. Well, this plane came in to do some strafing. Well, they caught us by surprise. So he did strafe and he went up and when he gets over at the other side these guys were loading up. These guys were already loaded up and he turned around and came back. I never saw an airplane disintegrate right in front of me. (Laughing) It just--it blew to pieces and then they sent another airplane and that plane never even came close. They, they never figured that we had guns on that thing. So that, that, that was, that was a really, an interesting thing to see. (Laughing) In fact, over on Guadalcanal there was a 150 Plane air raid. I forgot when that was--August. And we had 90-millimeter guns pointed up in the sky so what they did--they knew that gun somehow, they knew that that gun could not come down this way fast, so they sent dive bombing fighters to dive down real quick and then go like that. And this gun is still at a 45-degree angle and that plane is strafing so they could--that way they could knock out the gun and their plane could come below at 25,000 feet because they were up there real high. And so what they did, the 90-millimeters were like this, so a battery of two and there was four, 40-millimeters on each side. Two here, two here, two here and two here. So as these planes came down, that gun started to come down. These other guns were already sitting there because they couldn't shoot way up high. We'll just keep it for the low flying. Well, they were sitting over here and then when they knocked out the fighter planes these 90-millimeters were shooting up there--searchlights would hit a plane at 25,000, 22,000 feet or where ever it was and it would look like a--as soon as one searchlight would hit it another one would hit it. Pretty soon it would be four on them and it looked like a silver cross. It looked like you were in church--sitting way up in the sky and then all of a sudden over here, there was some little pink-like, flares, fireworks--plane wouldn't blow up. I thought, what the hells that. We couldn't figure that one out. The next night the same thing. Well they, they shot down 99 out of 120. Well a lot of it was the planes that went up after them, a lot of it was the 90-millimeters and once they chased them away from our area in Guadalcanal out over the ocean that's when these little sparks were coming out of the sky. We didn't know what it was. We went down to the airfield, at Henderson Field. They had a canvas thing over this airplane for about three or four days before--and the next day they had that canvas off. It was a big black airplane, looked like an overblown P-38. It was a P-61 night fighter. Well what happened, every time the radar put the other plane on the scope when he got within range, the guns went off automatically. And he shot down, I would say over--in front of our eyes about four or five. It was something.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: Tell him about the time that patrol got to close and hid behind the elephant leaf.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, we were on malaria control. We were on malaria control and usually about four people. We had two guys carrying cans of diesel fuel; two, 5-gallon cans. So 10-gallons of diesel fuel and the other two guys carried some--small explosive; jell ignite we called it--looked like spaghetti and our Thompson's. And they told us, if you see anything don't shoot cause your gonna bring others. And they--cause you're out somewhere way--we're here but you're way over there somewhere. We just had to roam around the island and look for stagnant water. Then what we'd do, we'd spray the diesel fuel all around the shore and it could be 50 foot square or it could be an acre. But you didn't have to use a lot of oil. Just spray around the shore because that's where the monopolies--mosquitos had their little breathing tubes. They weren't in the middle, they were in the shore of this body of water and they're trying to breathe. So when you oiled it up you suffocated them, they'd die. And it's only the female mosquito, not the male. And we heard a rumbling and talking and--and you could smell something like rotten socks. And what the heck is this and we--there were plants, I don't know what the heck the name is. We called them elephant ears; great big leaves like this and they usually curl like this. And so you can get behind them and poke your finger through there and you could see. Well we saw, well first we saw one Japanese and it looked like an officer. And the idiot that was next to me--don't make any noise, don't talk, don't even cock your rifle or gun or anything. I had a Thompson uncocked all the time--so the other guys name was Costa. What the hell was his first name. Anyway, he said don't shoot. Pretty soon about 12 guys with rifles came walking through there like this and went off over there. So we let 'em go. With two guns (Laughing) you ain't gonna argue with 12 guns and who knows what else is behind them. Because a lot of times what they'd do--they'd send one or two guys which were expendable so that you could shoot at them and then they'll send 10, 20 or 30 guys after you. And then later on the same day, I think it was--we heard like a troop of elephants. We said "what the hell is this." We're sitting there behind those leaves. Got the gun aimed--here comes a great big Marine about 250 pounds without a shirt on, just his helmet, shorts and a strap over his shoulder. And I didn't see what kind of a gun it was. And a big long pole with a net on the end of it. He was chasing butterflies. (Laughing)--So we jumped up and when I saw he was a Marine--as soon as we jumped out he's down on the ground and he goes over like this and he's got a double barrel shotgun. (Laughing)--He's aiming at us. Well then he told us about the butterflies and he showed us some. Boy, he says "you know" he said "I catch these, I chloroform 'em and I put em between this cotton," and he's got a couple of them and he shows us. Well those are worth seven hundred, six hundred and five hundred dollars each--for collectors. I said, "your kidding." Oh, he had--I mean some of them were like this and don't damage 'em. Keep them very chloroform and put the cotton gently over them. And there's the guy that almost got his head blown off. We almost got ours blown off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you want to tell him about the sniper or no?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh yeah. Then at Bougainville there was--a Japanese would be up in the tree and he covered himself with--looked like porcupine skin, died green with the needles, with the fur sticking out like this and when he put it over his head and he's up in a tree you couldn't see him. But we had a trick. A colorblind guy could tell real foliage from imitation foliage. So the Marines always had a colorblind guy, and we always had a colorblind guy that we knew was colorblind. Can tell brown from green and red. If there's different colors we didn't mess with them, but those especially. And the Marines, whenever they were cruising around what we call the front lines, which was really not a front line at all, it just--here was the fixed position that we were in--over there was like just jungle and then over on the other side was their fixed position. So these guys are cruising around with Dobermans and then if there--you're, you're following the native paths and if there's a clearing over here, if theres a clearing--when you come in, skirt the clearing. Never stand in the clearing cuz usually they had a sharp shooter up in the tree somewhere and he was told, aim for this whenever a guy hits the middle of the clearing. So if a guy got hit over here, you didn't rush to help him, he's dead. Just stay away from that spot. And if you're walking around and you see a clearing you stay away from that spot. Yeah, some guy got careless. He got hit in the forehead. And these two Marines with the Doberman let the Dobermans go and they're going around sniffing and when they get the tree that he went up on they're ready to peel the bark right off of it. So then they bring the guy, the colorblind guy and says, "you see anybody," and he's looking and looking, "yeah, over there." So you say, "you mean here." "No, no. Over there." "Oh, over on this branch." "No, no, the other one. Right in the middle, you see that foliage." "Yeah I see it. That ain't real." So they're looking like this and their taking their guns out and they're shooting and the guy says "you got a Thompson, you got bullets in that Thompson." I said "yeah, I got 50."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You had the gangster type.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And I got--what I did every fourth or fifth bullet I put a tracer. And in the daytime you don't have to aim you just put where that light goes. You don't use it at nighttime because it tells them where you are. I get up underneath here with these guys with the dogs. Had B-A-R's--and they each put in 20 bullets up there and I put about 40. Pretty soon splash splash--blood came down and somebody went up there and cut the guy down and it was a sniper. We got 'em. And one guy says "I think I got him." So the other guy says "I think I got 'em." I looked and I saw a couple of dark holes over here and I says, "I don't want to argue with you guys, but I think I got a couple too." (Laughing)--And then lets see--oh, then we went down to Australia. That was a nice place. (Laughing)--We, we went down there because we were all sick. I was down to about 117 pounds after dysentery and malaria and all that. Not enough food, good food. Too much work in the hot sun. So we, we went down to Australia to recuperate and while we were recuperating there was a subbase down at Brisbane. We took it all apart, boxed it, put it on a ship to go up to the Philippines when we got ready to go there. And then they kicked us out of Australia because instead of recuperating, we went out and got drunk every night. (Laughing)--Instead of gaining weight, we lost more weight. Then they, some--some went up by ship--they stopped at New Guinea. I went up, I flew--I went up from Brisbane to Milne Bay over here in New Guinea. Then I flew to Peleliu, then I flew to Sangley Point which is opposite Manila, at Manila Bay. Manila Bay came like this, little points sticking out--Corregidor was here. This is Sangley Point, Cavite and Manila was over here. That was a prewar Navy base in Cavite, and there was a real nice concrete prewar hospital built in 1908 when it was a U.S. Navy base and when the Japanese abandoned that, that area they took all their troops out and sent them over to Manila including Navy cause this was all Navy, Japanese Navy. There was one float plane left on this side of the island. We came in on this side and just as we landed we landed here by sea plane. We heard a couple of big booms. The U-shaped hospital, beautiful building. They put a 500 pound bomb here and 500 pound bomb there and blew up the two wings--collapsed all the floors. I think it was a three floor building and the guy who did that was running across here to hop onto the float plane and we're running over here after him and our guys shot him, shot the float plane, caught it on fire till it blew up. Till the pilot and him were killed but you should have seen that beautiful nice building. And in the town of Cavite which is right outside the Navy base there was an old mission church built by the Spanish back in the 1600's; beautiful building. They had nothing to do. The Japanese was using that as target practice, this beautiful historic building and they blew the front right off of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell them about the Black Sheep Squadron.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How you met the guys from the Black Sheep Squadron?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, that was on Vella LaVella. The big Marine Fire Squadron was--what the hecks that guys name?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Boyington?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, Pappy Boyington. He was there with the crew. The crew--the guys in his squadron were all alcoholics. (Laughing)--When they came off of an airplane--there's two guys there. One with a bottle, one with a big cup and he'd poured about that much and--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that's history.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not a shot the whole time.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --yeah, (Laughing) and these guys were anywhere from 21 to 51 it looked like.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get to know any of them?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Nah. Well, Boyington was the friendliest really, cause we built them a chow hall that was really nice. We built them a little officer's club which was real nice. Well, they give us a snort every now and then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But they fought a lot.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They fought a lot.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, and then what they would do, what his group would do see--there was VMF-211, VMF-214, VMF-208, I think it was. So VMF is fighter, fighters heavier than air. And it was then--there was ___ outfits which were the ones that maintained the airplanes. Well his ___ outfits were nice guys, the other ones were bums. If they got ahold of a trailer load of beer they invited you over to have a beer with them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I didn't know he knew Pappy Boyington.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And, whenever a ship came in with fresh fruit like, oranges-- oh, man. We always volunteered to help unload, get it out of here before night. When we unload--you know, one for you and one for me. One for you and one for me. (Laughing)--And we'd all--we'd park our trucks so that there was just walking space between them like about four feet, four feet another truck. And the driver sitting there waiting. So cigarettes, fresh fruit, beer. Over here we had a little round ring with a blade sticking out of here that we could slide--or over here we could slide up and we'd sharpen the blade. And if you're carrying these big boxes of cigarettes and you're walking slow your going shh, shh, shh, shh, shh. Make a little flap, pull out a carton when you get to your truck, there goes a carton of cigarettes. And beer, the same thing. So when ever we did that--if it was the--the VMF-211 or VMF-214, their ___ outfit that maintained their airplanes, says you guys going to unload, yeah we volunteered, well we'll help you. They'd send their guys down and we were all in on this cuz half of that stuff went to officers anyway and since they were nothing but a lazy bunch of people we figured they didn't deserve it so we're going to help ourselves.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: How about that MacArthur--when you built that hut?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, we--I got sent over, I got sent over to New Guinea. MacArthur went up there to inspect so they wanted this nice little shack for him. So we had drawings and everything--for like a little cabin. We precut the wood. We had to cut down the trees, make our own--we had a lumber mill cut the wood to size and everything, take it out there. We assembled this little cottage. It was, it was a sitting room with a veranda and a kitchen. And the veranda is where he had his--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Orange Juice.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --bed I guess to rest. So he went there early in the morning while we were there, three days before we put this up, beautiful kitchen, apartment size kitchen. The shack was about, about this big but one-and-a-half times or two-and-a-half times wider. I'd say about 20-by-20 and the veranda had a screen around it and everything. We had the whole thing--and a shower. But there was a bag of water up here and--but it had to be warmed. And he had to have his little cup of orange juice, fresh squeezed oranges. He had to have his liquor and like french toast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was his breakfast?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: That was--no, no, no, that was between breakfast and lunch.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Snack.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: A snack. And his and his pipe had to be sitting there. He comes up, looks around and of course everybody got chased away. He goes and sits down in this little hammock that we had set up over his veranda--takes a 45 minute nap, gets up, has some orange juice and leaves. That's what the hell we came over here to work on for three days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And the officers probably moved in.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Actually, you know the--Halsey made us sweat but he was good. If you needed it, he got it. MacArthur, if he needed it, he got it. MacArthur--I don't know what he did for his people but what he did for us we didn't like him at all. And when we were down--his headquarters were in Brisbane, Australia and you weren't allowed to go near it. I mean they had jeeps with guns on it and everything to get you away from there. That was his place over here next to it here was the American Red Cross building. Where there was a long line of people for--there was a long line of people to go up there because for screening.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Screening, right?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Then they also gave you the, the medicine for it. (Laughing)--Then they showed you the movie where they put it on the table--hit it with the hammer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They didn't really hit it with the hammer did they?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: No they, the old fashioned--they used a cork skew to pull it up. Anyway the prophylactic on the second floor of the Red Cross building. There's always a line out there and over here's MacArthur--boy--and that line ended right there and over here was a thing like downtown Cleveland where we have the soldiers and sailors monument.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: They had a similar type of a structure--Anzac Park, Anzac Square and Anzac is New Zealand--Australia troops that were in World War I. They had a great big beautiful park there. And you'd be walking down the street with a girl, the Australians across the street, the men--the men that were in the service--I would say about 80 percent of the young people were in the service but the old timers. Hey guys, give her a bloody ______+. That was a nice place. There was--there was a restaurant downtown in, in Brisbane called the New World Cafe--Chinese. You could get a steak, stikenittes,(ph) you could get a steak with 2 eggs sunny side up on top and home fries. And a cup of real American coffee not the kind that they had--67 cents. So instead of eating in the chow hall where we got mutton. Did you ever taste mutton?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: You don't want to taste mutton.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've heard about it.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: I think this was goat from World War I because it came out of tins. It was the most horrible food I've ever eaten so I would sneak into town we had a hole in the fence. And we'd go into town to the New World Cafe and get a steak and eggs, chips for--we called it french, or either french fries or home fries they called it chips and coffee with cream and sugar--67 cents. One of our chiefs had a brother who was captured out in the Philippines and they were using him for bayonet practice, (Coughing)--and all they had to do is put a Jap in front of him and look out. So if, if the Marines captured any Japanese and they had to be wounded in such a way that they couldn't do anything and what they did, put their hands behind their heads, tied their thumbs together on their neck--because those guys--the guy in front would have a gun strapped to his back and the guy behind him would be walking like this and the guy would bend over and he'd use the gun and shoot somebody. So a lot of the Marines--and I don't blame them. If they captured somebody they'd march them down to the stockade which is like a mile and a half a way down the road. Soon as they got around the bend out of sight you know, bam, bam and then they'd come back and say--that son of a gun he tried to run away. Well where was he going to run. But a lot of times like on Bougainville where we had the stockade there was one Marine officer who spoke English.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The Major?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And he, man he spoke as well as we did--American.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: He was raised in California or maybe Washington, Oregon but he knew our customs and he new the law and he new everything and he also figured Americans are kind, generous people. See here's a guard on him. "Give me a cigarette." He said "I only have one." "Well you got to give me a cigarette." "Who said so." "The Geneva Convention." And he's arguing with him and the guy said "well I'm going to light up the cigarette and smoke it." He says "no you're not, you're going to give it to me." Bam. "That's what I'm going to give you." Shot him dead. So, I mean there were a lot of bad things going on both ways. But like we always said--they started it. The American soldier is the kindest most generous guy there is. If you need help, he's there. If there's anyway he can help you, food or this or that, he'll do it. But don't get him angry. Cuz if you get American soldier or sailor or Marine angry they're the worst you've ever seen, let me tell you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, we left the Philippines--

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: They didn't tell you the war ended, remember?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --in November 1945.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They didn't tell you the war ended for a few weeks?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: They didn't. In August and September, they never told us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well you knew about the bombs being dropped right?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't know about any of that?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Nah. We knew nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just wanted you to finish your work?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: No, what they wanted us--what we were doing we were building sea plane ramps over in Cavite for the flying boats that Pan American Airways was going to use--and we were--we were working on this day and night and then they took all our old shot up equipment--we got new equipment. They took my Thompson which was by this time kind of worn. I got it back, it looked brand new. At first I thought it was a different gun but it was the same numbers--serial so they rebuild it. Well what we were doing we were getting set to--in fact what we just got through work--I was working on, was a 600 bed hospital, emergency hospital. This is for the invasion of Japan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Well when it was November when we found out all about this stuff and when we found out about it I got to thinking you know, you're on the way home, you're thinking. You know, they would of murdered us. And we would of murdered them. When somebody says you feel bad about dropping the bomb, I say "no." Well they killed 130,000 people, but we saved a million cause actually if we were building a 600 bed hospital in Cavite which was a small dot in Manila Bay on the other side--Baguio they were building a hospital in Lingayen, and they would build a hospital, they were expecting an awful lot of injured. The casualties would have been terrible including that--and then we were told--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: To not say the war was over.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --that you, you can't trust 'em. If he's a kid he's out to kill you so you got to get 'em. Well that meant shoot everybody. We would have--we would have killed, oh, we would have killed a million at least, but we would have lost.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There are a lot of side cases?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: So how many did we lose in Nagasake and Hiroshima?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: Initially?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah, all total.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 250,000 initially?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: We saved 3 million at least.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: At least. You know they had, over 6,000 planes hidden. Where did they think they were going to use them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They were going to hit the landing craft instead of the ships.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Plus they had--well I found out where we were gonna go. We were going to go to--if this is Japan over here--Kyushu.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He did five amphibious landings.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Five landings, is that your?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: No, we were going to go over on this side with the 4th Marines.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what what was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (female)
sp.p: He was sicker than a dog.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: He came home in November from the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (female)
sp.p: No, he came home in October.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: Was it October?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (female)
sp.p: Sure, cuz we got married in November and I still dont know what the big ______+

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: My discharge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's that--you have a copy of that?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: The kid on the gun?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The kid on the gun. The kid that you gave a cigarette to and the smoke came out of it?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah. On Vella LaVella when I got off the LST and this young dead Marine over here--I opened up his pack and his shirt, pants fit me. Mine were burned--I took 'em, and I'm going around looking for Mr. Gill because I was his bodyguard. I lost track of him. Further down they had set up at the beach--they put a tarp up to keep the sun off these guys. I, I see the doctors cutting off arms, cutting off legs. I think Holy Christ, What the hell is going on around here. This Doc he was our doctor actually. He, he and a--the corpsman I guess amputated at least a half a dozen legs, half a dozen arms, plus guys that were patched up--holes in them and everything they had them stretched out all over the place. And there's this one young guy over here. And he had a blanket up to here like this. And the tip of his nose was cut off like somebody just took a razor and just sliced it right off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And he, he says, he waved to me like this and I said, "what do you want" he says "can I have a cigarette?" And I said "yeah." So I took out a cigarette and he says "would you light it for me." So I lit it. He said "would you hold it in my mouth." I felt like telling him what the hells the matter with you. You want me to smoke it too. So I put it there and he took a puff. He took an inhale and I seen smoke coming out over here. And I put it there again and he took another inhale and I pick the blanket over and theres a hole about this big in him and he only took two puffs and he died. And the kid was only I didn't even think he was even 20 years old; a young Marine. That's I--I felt terrible for thinking you know, how rotten it was for him to ask for all this stuff when all he can do is hold it himself, he couldn't raise his arms, poor guy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I have this on tape for extra money you would disarm bombs.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Bomb disposal.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How much money would they pay you for bomb disposal?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: For each bomb?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: --a month.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: $5 a month?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah. If you're on bomb disposal.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker (male)
sp.p: Tell him about that 500 pounder how they were beating on it.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Oh, I'd go out on Guadalcanal one of our planes--SBD which carries a bomb underneath the belly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: On a wish bone. It got stuck and it was hanging there. Where ever he was going to bomb it never came off so they told him to ditch the plane over the ocean. The guy says "nope" the pilot always has the last word. He says, "nope, I'll come in." So when he came in, he came in like this and he bounced went up over here and the bomb slipped off then he landed. Well everybody runs to the bomb and I'm in a jeep when I saw what happened I was heading for the bomb and I see a guy sitting on it like a horse holding it, another guy hitting it with a hammer--he's hitting up on the nose. I turned that jeep around I went as fast as I could away and I heard a boom. And there was a circle of people over there when I was heading for it and there was nothing there when I turned around to look. And two of our guys the only thing the only way they identified them was--the tattoo from this guy was stuck on a tree about 50 feet away. Killed 40 idiots sitting there watching somebody hitting a nose of a bomb with a hammer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get any shows over there--any USO shows or anything?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Once, we got Kay Kaiser. Did you ever hear of Kay Kaiser, College of Musical Knowledge?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: College of Musical Knowledge, right.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: We got him and they put on a real good show for us and then one time we had Randolph Scott. Dressed like a cowboy and everything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh Wow.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Well, what they did they put up 55-gallon drums and then they put plywood across the top that was the stage. We had headlights of our trucks down from here and from there and from here and right in the middle of that we got an air raid. And they naturally turned off all the lights real quick and all you could here was Randolph Scott screaming. Help me. Help me. Help me, I don't want to die. We don't want to die either so shut up. Then when the air raid was over they put on the lights and everything and he gets up on the stage and he's going to show us how he can flip his guns and all this. Boo. Get out. Go home--let the dancers out. He was chicken.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: And we had visit us--we had--what the hell was this guys name--Tyrone Power.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: He was just going through. He was just--they just visited us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Actually, what he wanted was a drink and some good food.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Laughing.

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think we covered it?

sp.speaker: Denny Frangos
sp.p: Yeah. [End of Interview]
